what_it_does: Volumetric video — 3D point-cloud footage you can walk around in, like immersive VR content — requires enormous bandwidth to stream at full resolution; a single high-quality scene can demand 720 megabits per second. The natural fix is to send a lower-resolution version and then upscale it on the viewer's device, but existing 3D upscaling neural networks are far too slow for real-time use on mobile headsets. VoLUT replaces the neural-network inference step with a precomputed lookup table (a giant array of pre-answered questions), achieving 8.4x faster upscaling than the prior best system at the same visual quality, and reducing bandwidth by 70%.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A lookup table (LUT) stores pre-answered computations: given an input pattern, the answer is already in a table rather than computed fresh each time. For 2D image upscaling this trick is known, but 3D point clouds (collections of floating-point x,y,z positions in space rather than pixels on a grid) make indexing a table hard: you cannot simply look up a continuous coordinate.

Stage 1 — dilated interpolation. When a low-density cloud arrives, VoLUT first increases the number of points by interpolation (guessing new point locations between existing ones). Standard nearest-neighbor search looks only at the closest few points, which clusters new points near already-dense areas and creates visual artifacts. VoLUT uses dilated search: it considers the k*d nearest points (where d is a dilation factor, typically 2) and samples from that wider pool, spreading new points more evenly. An octree (a 3D spatial index that recursively subdivides a cube into eight sub-cubes) accelerates the search, and neighbor relationships computed for the original points are reused for the interpolated ones, avoiding redundant work. This gives a 3.7x to 8x speedup over naive interpolation alone.

Stage 2 — LUT refinement. The interpolated points are still imprecise. A small neural network was trained offline to predict a tiny position correction (offset) for each point given its local neighborhood of 4 neighbors. Instead of running that network at playback time, VoLUT precomputes its outputs for every possible quantized input. Each 3D coordinate is normalized to the range 0-1 relative to its neighborhood, then rounded into 128 discrete bins per axis. The four neighbors' binned coordinates are concatenated into a table index, and the stored offset is retrieved and applied — a single array lookup costing microseconds instead of seconds. The resulting table is about 1.6 GB (stored on-device), a practical trade-off for VR headsets with several gigabytes of RAM.

Adaptive streaming. A model-predictive-control algorithm (a planning method that optimizes quality over a short lookahead window) selects continuous-valued downsampling ratios each frame to match the available network bandwidth, rather than snapping to a small set of fixed quality levels.

The result. On a mobile-class device (Orange Pi, similar to a Meta Quest 3), VoLUT runs at 30+ frames per second; the prior neural approach ran far below real-time. End-to-end, it delivers 36.7% better quality-of-experience than the previous state of the art while consuming only 17% as much data on an LTE network.
